newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Macau airport may miss opportunity to boost business.
newsitem.headline: Macau airport may miss opportunity to boost business.

text.p: Macau International Airport denied suggestions that it is pricing itself out of the market and missing a golden opportunity to attract passenger and cargo airlines before Hong Kong's new airport opens.
A Macau airport spokesman said he was aware of the criticism but added that the airport is working hard to attract new business.
The under-achievement claims come from three senior executives who have wide experience of the aviation industry in Hong Kong and China.
"Macau has this window of opportunity and they are losing it," Jim Eckes, principal of aviation consultants Indoswiss Aviation told Reuters.

"Hong Kong is having to turn away more than a hundred flights a week and it is a perfect time for Macau to capitalise but I don't think they are. Macau said it is 15 percent cheaper to fly there than into Kai Tak but it is not enough," he said.

"They should be offering a 50 percent discount to attract as many airlines as possible before Hong Kong's new airport opens. After it opens and especially when the second runway is in use it will be too late for Macau," Eckes added.
Stephen Miller, former head of Hong Kong Dragon Airlines (Dragonair) and now managing director of The Trinity Group Limited, which specialises in aircraft leasing and aviation consultancy, agreed.

"Macau airport should have had a direct ferry link with Hong Kong to give passengers an easy connection. If that happened as initially promised it would not take that much longer to get to Macau than to Hong Kong's new airport and if fares were cheaper, passengers would go to Macau. Until there is better infrastructure Macau will always struggle," Miller said.
Gilbert Chow, general manager for Northwest Airlines and Hong Kong representative of the International Air Transport Association(IATA) also questioned whether Macau was doing enough.

"It costs US$3,200 to land and park a 747-400 at Kai Tak but Macau is only slightly cheaper. If they took a long term view and lowered fees they might be able to attract airlines away from Hong Kong and keep them even when Chek Lap Kok opens," Chow said.

The Macau airport spokesman said landing fees were on average 15 percent lower than at Kai Tak. The cost of landing a Boeing 747-400 in Macau is about U.S. 2,582 dollars with no peak or night surcharges or additional navigation, noise or lighting fees, he said.
"People seem to forget that Macau is a new airport and Kai Tak has been established for 40 years. It always takes time for growth and that is what is happening now," he added.
" A lot of new airports take 10 years to get to where we are now and airlines take time before committing to a new airport,"
the spokesman said. -Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542-7706 Fax+5017
